titre: The Nixon Shock, or the Improvised End of the Gold Standard (August 15, 1971)
accroche: One Sunday evening in 1971, Nixon announces on television the end of the dollar's convertibility into gold: twenty-seven years of monetary system stop all at once.
contenu_vulgarise:
On Sunday, August 15, 1971, in the evening, Americans turn on their televisions for a presidential address announced earlier that day with no details about its content. Richard Nixon presents what he calls his “new economic policy”: a 90-day freeze on wages and prices (the country is then dealing with 6.1% unemployment and inflation close to 6%), a 10% surcharge on imports, and a decision that is more discreet in its wording but far heavier in consequences: the suspension of the dollar's convertibility into gold. The decision was made two days earlier, on Friday, August 13, at a closed-door meeting at Camp David bringing together Federal Reserve chairman Arthur Burns, Treasury Secretary John Connally, his deputy Paul Volcker, and a dozen other advisers. The United States' main trading partners learn of it at the same time as the public, through television: American financial markets, for their part, are closed that Sunday.

## A system built on a 1944 promise

Since the Bretton Woods conference in July 1944, the international monetary system has rested on a double anchor: the currencies of the member countries are fixed against the dollar, and the dollar itself is convertible into gold at the rate of $35 an ounce for foreign central banks. As long as the United States holds most of the world's gold reserves, the promise holds effortlessly. But over the course of the 1960s (foreign spending, dollars piling up abroad), American gold reserves dwindle until, on August 15, 1971, they amount to about 10,000 metric tons, less than half their historical peak. Countries begin to ask for their dollars to be converted into gold, which Nixon interprets as a speculative attack on the American currency. His response is not to devalue by the book, by negotiating a new rate with the other countries in the system: it is to shut the window outright, overnight, and let the dollar float.

## The end of a system that never reopened

Nixon presents his decision as temporary: a suspension, not an abandonment. It never was: no convertibility has been restored since, and the Jamaica Accords, in 1976, officially ratify what August 15, 1971 had already decided in haste, floating exchange rates, determined by markets rather than fixed by a treaty. What strikes you, in hindsight, is the contrast between the scale of the break and the way it is decided: no international summit, no negotiation with partners, a handful of advisers gathered for two days in secret to end a system built twenty-seven years earlier by 44 countries brought together for three weeks. The dollar, since then, is no longer worth what gold is willing to say about it: it is worth what the markets decide, each day, that it is worth.

repere.texte: As of August 15, 1971, US gold reserves had fallen to about 10,000 metric tons (less than half their historical peak), which precipitated Nixon's decision to suspend the dollar's convertibility.

carte.punch: One Sunday evening in 1971, a televised speech ends 27 years of a dollar convertible into gold.
carte.idee: On August 15, 1971, Richard Nixon announces live the suspension of the dollar's convertibility into gold, decided two days earlier in secret at Camp David. Presented as temporary, the measure puts a definitive end to the monetary system set up at Bretton Woods in 1944.

quiz.question: Why does Nixon suspend the dollar's convertibility into gold on August 15, 1971?
choix: Because the US Congress had just passed a law requiring it
Because American gold reserves were running out in the face of foreign conversion requests
Because the 1944 Bretton Woods agreement expired that day
Because the Soviet Union had just devalued its own currency
quiz.explication: American gold reserves had fallen to less than half their peak after years of outflows of currency; Nixon chose to close convertibility rather than negotiate a devaluation, with no connection to a Congressional vote, a treaty deadline, or a Soviet decision.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Besides suspending the dollar's convertibility into gold, what other measures does Nixon announce on August 15, 1971?
choix: A general increase in income taxes on American households
A freeze on wages and prices, plus a surcharge on imports
The immediate closure of all of the country's commercial banks
Strict gasoline rationing across the national territory
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry cites the 90-day freeze on wages and prices and the 10% surcharge on imports as the two other measures announced that same evening, with no tax increase or bank closure.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who takes part in the secret Camp David meeting that decides to suspend the dollar's convertibility?
choix: The entire US Congress, gathered in special session
The G7 finance ministers, gathered in Washington
Arthur Burns, John Connally, and Paul Volcker, with a dozen other advisers
Treasury Secretary John Connally alone, with no other adviser
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The August 13 meeting at Camp David brings together Arthur Burns, John Connally, Paul Volcker, and a dozen advisers, not Congress or the G7, and not Connally alone.
